In February 2008 German tax investigators raided the home of the head of Deutsche Post, Klaus Zumwinkel, using client data stolen from a Liechtenstein bank. It opened one of the largest tax evasion cases in German history.

A former employee of the LGT bank, owned by the princely family, had sold data on hundreds of foreign account holders to the German intelligence service. Other countries, among them Britain and the United States, received data too.

Liechtenstein had lived for decades on foundations and trusts that hid wealth from foreign tax offices. Under pressure from Germany, the OECD and the EU, it agreed to share tax information. Like Switzerland, it gave up banking secrecy for foreign clients within a few years.
